narration.narration: Imagine walking into a Louisiana supermarket in 2026. Beside the beef is a blue package labeled “Lake Cow Bacon.” Outside, a yellow sign warns drivers about hippos crossing.
The local news is tracking another two-ton animal loose near a school. This America never existed. But in 1910, a Louisiana congressman asked Washington to build it.

His proposal promised to solve two emergencies with one animal: cheap meat for crowded American cities and open waterways for the South. The animal was the hippopotamus. The bill was real. The hearing was serious.
And today, another country has accidentally run part of the experiment for us. That evidence exposes what the proposal's confident witnesses could not yet see.

At the beginning of the twentieth century, American families were angry about the price of meat. Cattle supplies, feed costs, and powerful meatpackers all became targets as beef grew harder for working families to afford.

Louisiana had a different emergency. Water hyacinth—an ornamental plant imported from South America—had escaped into Southern waterways. It spread into thick floating mats, slowed boats, interfered with fishing, and resisted efforts to remove or burn it.

Representative Robert F. Broussard looked at expensive meat, a plant nobody wanted, and thousands of acres of warm wet habitat. To him, the crises appeared to fit together like two pieces of a machine.

In March 1910, Broussard brought House Resolution 23261 before the House Committee on Agriculture. It sought 250,000 dollars—about eight million in 2023 purchasing power—to import useful wild animals into the United States. Hippos would be the star.

Release them into Louisiana and Florida. Let them consume the unwanted vegetation. When they grew large, turn them into an affordable new meat supply. Supporters gave the product a friendlier name: lake cow bacon.

Broussard arrived with men whose biographies made the scheme feel adventurous rather than absurd: American scout Frederick Russell Burnham, South African soldier Fritz Duquesne, and Agriculture Department researcher William Newton Irwin.
They described hippo meat as rich, usable food and argued that the animals could thrive on waterfront farms. Even former president Theodore Roosevelt supported the broader idea.
For a country anxious about food, the pitch had a seductive shape: no sacrifice, no rationing—just turn one invasion into dinner.
Then the proposal grew larger. Irwin told the committee that imported animals could add as much as one million tons of meat to the national supply. Hippos were only the opening act.
Antelope might live on family farms. African buffalo could range across the West. Yaks could occupy the Rockies. Rhinoceroses were imagined in the Southwest.

It was an agricultural version of redesigning a continent: move animals to whatever American landscape resembled their old home, then harvest the result. Newspapers debated the idea. Supporters treated public disgust as a failure of imagination.
Americans already ate cattle that had once been foreign imports. Why should a hippo be different? The answer depended on two questions the committee was about to ask.
First: could hippos be contained on ordinary farms? Second: would they actually eat the water hyacinth? Broussard’s side answered yes to both.

They pictured manageable animals living behind fences on small waterfront properties, feeding on dense mats of free vegetation. From inside the hearing room, those answers completed the machine. Plant becomes hippo. Hippo becomes meat.
Two public problems disappear. But the machine was built around an animal they did not understand and a plant with almost no nutritional value. Modern evidence changes both answers.
Hippos spend their days in water, but that does not mean water plants are their normal fuel. At night they climb onto land and graze—often traveling miles for grass.
Aquatic plants make up only a small portion of their diet. And water hyacinth is roughly 95 percent water. An animal trying to live on it would process enormous bulk for very little energy.
So picture the first Louisiana herd after the novelty fades. The hippos do not remain politely inside a carpet of hyacinth. They leave the water after dark searching for grass.
They move along banks, through crops, across roads, and toward new waterways. Now add containment. Adult hippos are territorial, immensely powerful, and dangerous around boats and shorelines.

A fence that holds cattle is not proof against a determined animal weighing several thousand pounds. Every escape turns a farm problem into a public one. Their waste also moves nutrients from land into water.
In an African ecosystem, that flow is part of a long-established food web. In a foreign river, concentrated nutrients can change oxygen levels, algae, fish, and water quality.

The original promise was that hippos would repair an invaded ecosystem. The more plausible result is that America would add a mobile megaherbivore to the invasive plant it already could not control. That is an informed counterfactual.
But it is not merely imagination, because a version of it began in Colombia.

In the 1980s, drug trafficker Pablo Escobar imported four hippos for a private zoo at Hacienda Nápoles. After his death, most exotic animals were moved. The hippos were difficult to capture, so they remained. They bred.
Some left the estate. Their descendants spread through the Magdalena River basin. By 2026, the population was estimated at around two hundred animals.

Scientists have documented rapid population growth and warned about altered water chemistry, habitat disturbance, conflict with people, and pressure on native species. Colombia has tried sterilization, relocation, confinement, and euthanasia planning—each expensive, difficult, or politically painful.

Four founders did not need to be domesticated. They only needed warm water, grass, room to spread, and time. Now move that lesson north. Broussard was not proposing four animals behind a private fence.

His vision required a food industry: breeding stock, waterfront farms, transport routes, workers, slaughter facilities, and repeated contact between people and hippos. It also imagined releases across landscapes already struggling with an invasive species.
Colombia cannot tell us exactly what 1910 Louisiana would have become. It can tell us that “we will control them later” is not a plan.

Back in Washington, the Agriculture Committee did not send America rushing toward hippo ranches. Members remained unconvinced, and the proposal was shelved. There was no dramatic national vote that defeated hippo bacon by a handful of ballots.
That version makes a better legend, but the documented ending is quieter: the plan failed to advance. Broussard considered trying again.

Then his political ambitions shifted toward the Senate, World War I transformed American priorities, and meat production changed. The hippo idea slipped from public policy into historical trivia. That quiet ending is exactly why the story matters.
Catastrophe does not always end with a heroic rescue. Sometimes it ends with skepticism in a committee room, an unanswered practical question, and a folder placed on a shelf.
So return to that alternate grocery store. The lake cow bacon looks like proof that Broussard succeeded.

But follow the package backward and the rest of the world comes with it: fenced bayous, dangerous night grazing, altered rivers, costly control programs, and communities forced to live with a decision made generations earlier.
Hippo meat itself was never the impossible part. People have eaten it. Witnesses in 1910 said it tasted somewhere between familiar meats.
The impossible promise was that America could import a powerful animal, aim it at an ecological problem, and receive only the benefit. The package disappears. The warning sign disappears.
The grocery case returns to the one we know. History is usually explained by what people built—the laws they passed, the machines they invented, the animals they domesticated.
But our world is also shaped by plans that stopped before they became normal. The strangest thing in this meat aisle is not what is here. It is the product a skeptical committee kept off the shelf.
